newsitem.title: FRANCE: Juppe faces call for dismissal after French poll.
newsitem.headline: Juppe faces call for dismissal after French poll.

text.p: A heavyweight member of France's ruling centre-right coalition made a thinly-veiled call for Prime Minister Alain Juppe's dismissal on Monday after voters delivered a stinging rebuff to the government.

The Socialists, who with the leftist bloc won the first round of a snap parliamentary election on Sunday, confidently predicted President Jacques Chirac would not oppose dropping liberalism if he had to share power with a Socialist premier.

French financial markets tumbled, the franc slipped and many leading stock market futures also dropped in general nervousness at uncertainty over next Sunday's run-off ballot. The franc slipped to 3.3773 per mark.
As the right licked its wounds, National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin, a leading Euro-critic in Juppe's Gaullist RPR party, hinted that dropping the unpopular premier could help.

"You don't change campaign leaders in the middle of the watch, but given that one of the best hypotheses is that the centre-right could win a majority of a few seats (in the second round), the problems at stake are different from those posed by a hundred-seat advance," Seguin said on RTL radio.
"My forecast, and it has always been the same, is that the margin will be of five or six seats," he said. The centre-right could manage this provided it gave "clear answers" to the voters' message.
But former budget minister Nicolas Sarkozy, also an RPR member, said making Juppe the sole issue in the first round result would be missing the point.
"Looking for a scapegoat would not allow us to find the true answers to the citizens' discontent. The ruling coalition as a whole has been taught a lesson," he told France-Inter radio.

The left pledged vigorous state job-creation measures and a shorter working week without loss of pay to attack record 12.8 percent unemployment. The coalition promised market reforms to scale down state control, cut taxes and free private enterprise.
Ministers have acknowledged a "warning" across the government's bows in a protest vote against two years of austerity, high taxes and rising unemployment.
The vote put pressure on Chirac to intervene again in the election, in wnich he gambled his presidency 10 months before his giant parliamentary majority needed to face voters.

"Naming a new prime minister would appear like capitulation to the enemy," said political commentator Alain Duhamel. "Chirac could however give two or three personalities a more prominent role, like (former premier) Edouard Balladur or Seguin."
Socialist ex-labour minister Martine Aubry predicted few difficulties if France was forced into a new bout of "cohabitation", or power-sharing.
"If France chooses a leftist majority...I'm convinced Chirac will follow the trend set by France and the majority of the French people. I don't see any great difficulties," she said.

With many constituencies facing a run-off between the left and the far-right after the anti-immigrant National Front won 15 percent of the vote, ruling coalition leaders were meeting on Monday to debate what advice to give voters.
The Front said it aimed to become kingmaker. Its leaders were meeting on Monday morning to decide who to back in the run-off, if any one.

With most votes counted in metropolitan France, the Interior Ministry said the combined left had polled 40.1 percent, the RPR-UDF coalition and other right-wing candidates 36.5 percent and the Front 15 percent. Ecologists scored 6.8 percent.
Most of the 577 National Assembly seats were set to go to a run-off, where the behaviour of Front supporters and of the 31.6 percent of voters who abstained will be crucial.

Like Juppe, most cabinet ministers and centre-right leaders were forced into runoffs in their constituencies, some such as ex-president Valery Giscard d'Estaing and Paris mayor Jean Tiberi for the first time in their parliamentary careers.
